idiom_name: shm_open + ftruncate + mmap(MAP_SHARED), name travels in the message header
implementation_notes: Producer and consumer share a POSIX shared-memory object: shm_open creates or opens it by name, ftruncate fixes its length and mmap(MAP_SHARED) maps it, so the payload is written once into memory that both processes can read; the object name is what the message carries. Cleanup belongs to the pattern: shm_unlink removes the name while existing mappings keep working, so the consumer that claims the data must unlink it once it has read it.
pitfalls: The segment length is fixed by ftruncate: a payload that grows later needs a new object (and a new name in the message).
Shared memory has no access control beyond the file mode and the host-wide name space: any process that can open the name can read the payload, so an opaque name is not a secret.
shm_unlink only drops the name - a process that already mapped the segment keeps reading it, so "deleted" payloads can survive in stragglers.
Crashing between create and unlink leaves the object in /dev/shm (and in the kernel's limits) for the next run to trip over.

variants.name: Descriptor passing over an AF_UNIX socket (SCM_RIGHTS)
variants.implementation_notes: When the two ends already talk over an AF_UNIX socket, the payload can be an ordinary file (or shared-memory object) and the claim check becomes the open file descriptor itself: sendmsg/recvmsg with an SCM_RIGHTS ancillary message transfers a reference to the open file description, which the receiver maps with mmap or reads with pread. The reference is a capability - it disappears when the last descriptor closes - so there is no name that other processes can guess or attach to.
variants.idiom_name: sendmsg/recvmsg with SCM_RIGHTS, the passed descriptor is the claim check
pitfalls: A descriptor survives only as long as some process keeps it open: if the receiver fails to duplicate or hold it, the payload is gone when the sender exits.
Truncating the ancillary buffer (or never enabling SO_PASSCRED style checks) silently closes excess descriptors, so the failure looks like a missing payload rather than a protocol bug.
Nothing prevents leaking descriptors: every failed recvmsg path that does not close what it received drains the file-descriptor table.
FD passing works only between processes on the same host with a Unix-domain socket; a bridged or networked hop cannot carry the capability.
